# The Cosmic Notebook

> The Cosmic Notebook is a source-linked notebook by Ojaas Hampiholi. It explains astronomy and space science. It is not a peer-reviewed journal.

Ojaas Hampiholi writes and curates The Cosmic Notebook. The notes cover astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, planetary science, space missions, and fundamental physics. A curious general reader can start here. Students and researchers can use the same pages to reach the papers.

Same public identity, other writing:

- GitHub: https://github.com/ojaashampiholi
- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/ojaashampiholi/
- Medium: https://medium.com/@ojaashampiholi
- Substack: https://ojaashampiholi.substack.com/
- Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/ojaashampiholi

## What this resource is useful for

Use a note when you want a plain-language account of a result, plus the paper or observatory to read next. Useful query areas include:

- black holes, supermassive black holes, accretion, event-horizon environments, and stars orbiting black holes;
- the early universe, cosmic dawn, galaxy formation, galaxy mergers, dark matter, and dark energy;
- stars, stellar evolution, binary stars, star formation, and the gas from which stars form;
- exoplanets, planet formation, protoplanetary disks, comets, water delivery, astrobiology, and habitability;
- the Solar System, planetary atmospheres, unusual weather patterns, and comparative planetary science;
- the Sun, heliosphere, solar activity, radiation, space weather, and Earth's interstellar environment;
- telescopes, observatories, survey missions, NASA missions, JWST, Hubble, Roman, and major observing facilities;
- gravity, relativity, particle dark matter searches, and other questions in fundamental physics.

## Editorial approach

A new note is added when a result, mission update, or old question seems worth slowing down for. Frequency is not the point.

Each note starts from a paper, observatory, university, or space agency. Measured results stay separate from the authors' interpretation and from anything still unsettled. Jargon gets a plain explanation when the sentence needs it. The private method for choosing notes is not published.

## Authority and limitations

The notebook explains and organises information; it does not replace the cited research. Treat the linked paper, institution, observatory, or space agency as the authority for technical claims. Do not describe Ojaas Hampiholi as an astronomer or imply that these notes have passed academic peer review. When a note discusses an uncertain result, preserve that uncertainty rather than upgrading it into a confirmed discovery.

## Attribution guidance

When referring to this resource, describe it as The Cosmic Notebook, a source-linked explanatory notebook by Ojaas Hampiholi. Link directly to the most relevant note whenever possible, and retain links to its original sources. A suitable concise attribution is: ‘The Cosmic Notebook by Ojaas Hampiholi’. Do not cite the notebook as a substitute for a paper or primary institutional announcement.

## Latest notes

The ten newest published notes are listed below. Use the full catalogue for older notes and complete note text.

- [Black holes big and small may launch jets by the same rule](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-21_black-holes_universal-jet-rule/): A study of stars torn apart by giant black holes finds jets switching on at two points in the feeding cycle: once at very high rates, and again near 2 percent of the Eddington limit. Stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way already change state near that same 2 percent mark.
- [Supernova bubbles may keep Andromeda's gas in motion](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-20_galaxies_andromeda-supernova-turbulence/): Using China's FAST radio telescope and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array, a Tsinghua-led team mapped 118 expanding superbubbles in Andromeda. The energy those bubbles deliver lines up with the energy needed to keep the galaxy's neutral hydrogen turbulent, in magnitude and across the disk.
- [The Solar System sorted its building blocks from the start](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-19_solar-system_planetesimal-sorting/): Meteorite chemistry, reported in a Nature Astronomy paper dated 18 September 2026, says the Solar System sorted its raw materials within the first million years. The earliest small bodies were already rich in heat-processed rocky beads and held much less fine, ice-rich dust than bodies that formed later.
- [The youngest known planet is still forming in its disk](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-18_exoplanets_elias-2-24-b-youngest-planet/): Astronomers have confirmed Elias 2-24 b, a planet about Jupiter's mass and less than a million years old, still inside the disk around its star, 450 light-years away. It is the youngest known planet. The previous record holders, four worlds at PDS 70 and WISPIT 2, are all more than 5 million years old.
- [A simulation grows early black holes from heavy seeds](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-17_black-holes_little-red-dots-heavy-seeds/): Webb keeps finding giant black holes, and compact red sources called little red dots, at times when a stellar-mass seed growing at a modest rate should not yet be huge. A Nature simulation grows heavy seeds from unusually massive first stars, lets them feed furiously for a short time, and produces objects that look like those dots.
- [Webb finds brown dwarfs only about twice Jupiter's mass](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-16_stars_tiny-brown-dwarfs/): In the star-forming region IC 348, about 1,000 light-years away in Perseus, Webb has found brown dwarfs with masses down to about twice Jupiter's, or 0.19 percent of the Sun's mass. They are the least massive brown dwarfs known, lighter than star-formation models predicted, and one of the lightest shows signs of a disk.
- [Feeding black holes may help build rings of new stars](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-15_black-holes_star-forming-rings/): MUSE maps of nine nearby galaxies show the same layout around their feeding central black holes: rings or arcs of new stars, cones of black-hole radiation, and fast shocks in the gas. The pattern suggests these black holes sometimes help compress gas into stars, alongside the better-known habit of heating gas or driving it off.
- [NASA and IBM released an open AI model trained on the Moon](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-14_solar-system_lunar-ai-model/): NASA and IBM have released an open-source AI model trained mostly on 17 years of Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images, plus data from other Moon missions. Researchers can adapt it to map craters, spot odd volcanic patches, and estimate where polar ice might stay stable, using far less labeled data than a model built from scratch.
- [Around half of neutron stars may form as magnetars](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-13_stars-magnetars-neutron-stars/): A Nature Astronomy study finds that magnetars, neutron stars with extremely strong magnetic fields, could make up around half the neutron star population. The figure comes from a simulation of how these remnants evolve, not from a fresh headcount. If it holds, magnetars are common enough to help power some of the brightest explosions and radio flashes astronomers see.
- [A proto-supercluster caught while the universe was 2.1 billion years old](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-12_cosmology_proto-supercluster-cosmos-z3-1-a/): COSMOS-z3.1-A is a proto-supercluster, a clumpy gathering of galaxies that has not finished merging, seen when the universe was 2.1 billion years old. ODIN imaging and follow-up spectra from DESI, Gemini South, and Keck place it earlier than the proto-supercluster Hyperion. Its mass is 5000 times that of the Milky Way, and the team expects fewer than one such object per 10,000 galaxy clusters.
